food.text: Under Muslim rule, farming in the Iberian peninsula flourished. The archaeozoologist Simon Davis writes that new irrigation techniques and new plants arrived, including sugar cane, rice, cotton, spinach, pomegranates and citrus trees.

The Caliphate of Córdoba traded widely around the Mediterranean, including with Christian lands. Its trade goods included essential foodstuffs such as grain, olive oil and wine, along with ceramic containers for storing perishables.

Medieval Arab historians and geographers described al-Andalus as fertile and prosperous, with abundant water and plenty of fruit. Trees such as the olive and the pomegranate were especially associated with the land.

Improvements in irrigation, such as the saqiyah waterwheel, and in animal husbandry made agriculture in al-Andalus far more productive. Archaeological evidence shows these changes supported population growth, urbanisation and a more stratified society.

In the tenth century, the Jewish scribe Menahem Ben Saruq wrote to the Khazar king about al-Andalus. He called it a land of corn, oil and wine, of fruits and all manner of delicacies, with pleasure-gardens, orchards and white mulberry trees on which the silkworm feeds.

The ninth-century writer Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Musa al-Razi, quoted later by al-Maqqari, described al-Andalus as a rich land with good, arable soil and fertile settlements. He wrote that it flowed copiously with plentiful rivers and fresh springs.

Western historians have wondered whether the medieval Arab writers were reliable, since they had a motive to stress the splendour of al-Andalus. Yet evidence from archaeology has broadly supported their claims of a fertile, productive land.
Seville became what Simon Davis calls a Mecca for agronomists. Its hinterland, the Aljarafe, served as their laboratory.

art.text: Italy has the richest concentration of Late Antique and medieval mosaics in the world. Many Italian mosaics were probably made by imported Greek-speaking artists and craftsmen. Surprisingly few significant mosaics remain in the core Byzantine territories.
art.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

art.text: By about the 10th century, Italy had lost the ability to produce high-quality mosaic work. The best work was created by teams despatched by Byzantine Emperors as diplomatic favours. Local craftsmanship only began to revive in the late 11th century.
art.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

art.text: During the period of Byzantine iconoclasm, 730-843, the vast majority of icons were destroyed. So little remains that any discovery sheds new understanding. Most of the surviving works are in Italy, in Rome and Ravenna, or at Saint Catherine's Monastery in Egypt.

Four churches in Rome have mosaics of saints placed near where their relics were held. All four abandon classical illusionism for large-eyed figures floating in space. The change may be explained by Rome having been in Byzantine hands from 536-545.
art.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

art.text: Justinian's octagonal church of San Vitale in Ravenna was built in the 6th century. It later inspired the Palatine Chapel in Aachen, constructed between 792 and 805, showing how far an Italian church's influence travelled.

The saints' mosaics in Rome span the 6th and 7th centuries. San Lorenzo fuori le Mura dates to the 580s, Sant'Agnese fuori le mura to 625-38, and Santo Stefano Rotondo to the 640s. The chapel of San Venanzio in the Lateran Basilica dates to about 640.
art.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

art.text: The only 8th-century mosaics known in Italy were in the tomb chapel of Pope John VII in Old St Peter's. They were recorded in drawings before the building was demolished, and some fragments were salvaged. Around a central Virgin Orans, with the Pope kneeling to her, were three registers of scenes from the Life of Christ.
art.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

war.text: Emperor Justinian's generals Belisarius and Narses conquered the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy after years of warfare that ended in 552. This conflict, known as the Gothic Wars, destroyed much of the town life that had survived the barbarian invasions. Towns lived on, but they became smaller and considerably more primitive than in classical Roman times. Wars, famines and disease epidemics had a dramatic effect on the demographics of Italy, and most people were left living by subsistence agriculture.

In 711 the Muslim Umayyad Caliphate crossed into the Iberian Peninsula from Northern Africa. A Visigothic clan had invited it to help rise against King Roderic. Between 711 and 788 the Umayyads conquered most of the Visigothic kingdom of Hispania and established the territory known as Al-Andalus.

In 773 Charlemagne, king of the Franks, crossed the Alps and invaded the Lombard kingdom, which covered all of Italy except the Duchy of Rome, Venice and the Byzantine possessions in the south. In June 774 the kingdom collapsed and the Franks became masters of northern Italy.

Totila, the Ostrogoth king, was killed at the Battle of Taginae, and the Byzantine general Narses then captured Rome and besieged Cumae. The new king Teia gathered the remnants of the army to relieve Cumae, but in October 552 Narses ambushed him at Mons Lactarius in Campania, near Mount Vesuvius. The battle lasted two days and Teia was killed in the fighting. Ostrogothic power in Italy was eliminated.

In 846 Muslim Arabs invaded Rome, looted St. Peter's Basilica and stole all the gold and silver in it. In response, Pope Leo IV began building the Leonine walls around the Vatican City in 847. They were completed in 853.

Most of the Exarchate of Ravenna finally fell under Lombard rule in 751, as the Byzantine Empire weakened under the pressure of the Muslim conquests. Former Exarchate states the Lombards did not conquer, such as the Duchy of Naples, became de facto independent, with ever less interference from the Eastern Roman Empire.

The Umayyad conquest of Hispania met resistance. A revolt during the conquest established the Christian Kingdom of Asturias in the north of the Peninsula. This began the long conflict between Muslim and Christian states known as the Reconquista.

Tariq ibn Ziyad led 12,000 men, mostly Berbers, across the strait in 711. Two years after the fall of Tangier, the Berber commander Tarif ibn Malik had already made the first incursions into Iberia, showing how Berber soldiers fuelled the conquest of the west.

According to the Roman historian Procopius of Caesarea, Narses let the Ostrogothic population and their Rugian allies live peacefully in Italy under Roman rule after his victory. With no real authority in Italy, the Franks and Alemanni invaded, but they were defeated at the Battle of the Volturnus. The peninsula was briefly reintegrated into the empire.

When Charlemagne's conquest brought down the Lombard kingdom in 774, the south stayed under Lombard control. The Duchy of Benevento was changed into the independent Principality of Benevento. Charlemagne called himself king of the Lombards and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800.

By the time of Justinian's death, the Byzantines controlled most of Italy, North Africa and a small foothold in southern Spain. Historians have criticised his reconquests for overextending the empire. His successors struggled partly because the essentially civilian nature of the empire made raising troops difficult.

In 951 King Otto I of Germany, already married to Queen Adelaide of Italy, invaded the Kingdom of Italy and proclaimed himself king. He defeated the previous king and conquered Pavia in 961. He then continued on toward Rome.

In 827 Muslim Arabs known as Aghlabids invaded and conquered Sicily. Their descendants, the Kalbids, ruled the island until 1053. In the late 9th century, the Byzantines and the Franks launched a joint offensive against the Arabs in southern Italy.

literature.text: Boethius wrote On the Consolation of Philosophy in 523 during a one-year imprisonment, while awaiting trial and eventual execution for the alleged crime of treason under the Ostrogothic King Theodoric the Great. He had been at the heights of power in Rome and was brought down by treachery. In 1891 Hugh Fraser Stewart called the work "by far the most interesting example of prison literature the world has ever seen."

Isidore of Seville compiled the Etymologiae, an encyclopedia, towards the end of his life, encouraged by his friend Braulio, Bishop of Saragossa. It became a widely used textbook throughout the Middle Ages. It was so popular that it was read in place of many of the classics it summarized, and some of those ceased to be copied and were lost.

Boethius's Consolation is prosimetrical, meaning it alternates sections of prose with sections of metered verse. In it he shows a virtuosic command of the forms of Latin poetry. It is classified as a Menippean satire, a fusion of allegorical tale, platonic dialogue and lyrical poetry.

Boethius set out to translate the entirety of the Greek classics for Western scholars, hoping to reconcile Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He published transcriptions and commentaries on works by Nicomachus, Porphyry and Cicero. He also wrote manuals on music, astronomy, geometry and arithmetic to pass Greco-Roman culture to future generations.

Cassiodorus, who served Theodoric the Great, founded the Vivarium monastery and wrote his Institutiones to guide the monks' studies. It offered an introduction to both divine and secular writings, in place of a Christian school he had planned in Rome. He is rivalled only by Boethius in his drive to preserve classical literature in the 6th century.

The first Arabic book on agronomy to reach al-Andalus, in the tenth century, was Ibn Wahshiyya's Nabatean Agriculture, which came from Iraq. It was followed by books written in al-Andalus itself, such as Al-Zahrawi's Abridged Book of Agriculture from Cordoba, around 1000 AD.

In Book II of the Consolation, Philosophy shows the capricious nature of Fate by describing the wheel of Fortune. She argues that true happiness lies in the pursuit of wisdom. Boethius had held the office of magister officiorum in Rome and was brought down by treachery, which inspired the work.

Boethius wrote De institutione musica toward the beginning of the sixth century. It later helped medieval theorists, from the ninth century onwards, understand ancient Greek music. Like his Greek predecessors, he believed arithmetic and music were intertwined and together showed the order and harmony of the universe.

The earliest surviving T and O map appears in a late 7th- or early 8th-century copy of Isidore of Seville's De natura rerum. It shows the known world as a circle divided in three by the Mediterranean, the Tanais and the Nile. A more detailed variation was drawn by Beatus of Liébana, an 8th-century Spanish monk, in his Commentary on the Apocalypse.

Paul the Deacon drew on the Origo gentis Langobardorum, the Liber pontificalis, the lost history of Secundus of Trent and the lost annals of Benevento. He also made free use of works by Bede, Gregory of Tours and Isidore of Seville.

From the ninth century, hundreds of Latin songs were recorded in neumes, including settings of the poems in Boethius's Consolation. Their music was long thought lost, because the notation gave only melodic outlines. After research by Sam Barrett, the ensemble Sequentia premiered reconstructed songs at Pembroke College, Cambridge, in April 2016.

In Book I of the Etymologiae, Isidore derives the Latin word for letters, littera, from the words for to read, legere, and road, iter, as if the term were legitera. His reasoning was that letters offer a road for people who read.

science.text: Boethius, a Roman senator who advised Theodoric the Great, set out to pass on Greco-Roman culture by writing manuals on music, astronomy, geometry and arithmetic. His De institutione musica, written near the start of the sixth century, later helped medieval theorists from the ninth century onward understand ancient Greek music.

Isidore of Seville compiled the Etymologiae, an encyclopedia, toward the end of his life, encouraged by his friend Braulio, Bishop of Saragossa. It covered mathematics, geometry, astronomy, medicine, metals, rocks, agriculture and tools, and three of its books drew largely on Pliny the Elder's Natural History.

Abbas ibn Firnas, who lived in Córdoba and died in 887, was an Andalusi polymath: inventor, astronomer, physician, chemist, engineer, musician and poet. He devised a way to make colourless glass and made magnifying lenses for reading, known as reading stones.

Under Umayyad rule, Córdoba, capital of the Emirate and then Caliphate of Córdoba, was transformed into a centre of education and learning. By the 10th century it had grown to be the second-largest city in Europe.

The Schola Medica Salernitana in Salerno was founded in the 9th century and rose to prominence in the 10th, becoming the most important source of medical knowledge in Western Europe. Arabic medical treatises were translated into Latin at Montecassino, supplementing the lore of Hippocrates, Galen and Dioscorides.

A T and O map shows the known world as a circle divided into three parts by a T formed from the Mediterranean, the river Tanais (Don) and the Nile. The earliest surviving example appears in a late 7th- or early 8th-century copy of Isidore of Seville's De natura rerum.

Ibn Firnas made glass planispheres and built an apparatus of linked objects that simulated the motions of the planets and stars. He also developed a way of cutting rock crystal, which let al-Andalus stop exporting quartz to Egypt to be cut.

Maslama al-Majriti, active under Al-Hakam II, was called the best mathematician and astronomer of his time in al-Andalus by Said al-Andalusi. He introduced new surveying methods with his colleague ibn al-Saffar and built a school of astronomy and mathematics that marked the beginning of organized scientific research in al-Andalus.

The Etymologiae was so popular that it was read in place of many of the classics it summarized, and some of those originals ceased to be copied and were lost. Almost 1000 manuscript copies survive, and the earliest is a 7th-century fragment of Book XI held at Saint Gall.

Some seven centuries after Ibn Firnas's death, Al-Maqqari wrote that Ibn Firnas covered himself with feathers, attached wings to his body and flung himself off a height. He is said to have flown a considerable distance, but his back was very badly hurt when he landed, because he did not know that birds come down on their tails and forgot to give himself one. Al-Maqqari cites no source for this, but says a verse by the court poet Mu'min ibn Saïd, written under Muhammad I, alludes to the flight: "He flew faster than the phoenix in his flight when he dressed his body in the feathers of a vulture." No other surviving sources refer to the event.
Beatus of Liébana, an 8th-century Spanish monk, drew a more detailed variation of the T and O map. It appears in the prologue to his Commentary on the Apocalypse and is known as the Beatus map.
Ibn Firnas introduced the Sindhind to al-Andalus, which had an important influence on astronomy in Europe. He also designed a water clock called the al-Maqata and a prototype for a kind of metronome.

politics.text: In 568 the Lombards entered Italy and tried to recreate a barbarian kingdom in opposition to the Byzantine Empire. They took authority over much of the peninsula. The Exarchate of Ravenna and the duchies of Rome, Venetia, Naples and the southernmost portions stayed outside their control.
The Visigothic kingdom of Hispania lasted from 507 to 711. Its Arianist Visigoths were converted to Catholicism along with their king Reccared in 587.

In 711 the Umayyad Caliphate crossed from Northern Africa into Iberia at the invitation of a Visigothic clan that wanted help rising against King Roderic. By 788 the Umayyads had conquered most of the Visigothic kingdom and established Al-Andalus. A revolt during the conquest founded the Christian Kingdom of Asturias in the north.
On 25 December 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as Roman Emperor. The title had not been used for more than three centuries, since the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476.

The Byzantine Empire reached its greatest extent under Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565 and briefly reconquered much of Italy and the western Mediterranean coast. A plague that began around 541 was devastating: it killed a large proportion of the population and severely reduced the empire's social and financial stability. Long warfare with Persia added fiscal and military strain.

In 773 Charlemagne crossed the Alps and invaded the Lombard kingdom, which held all of Italy except the Duchy of Rome, the Republic of Venice and the Byzantine south. By June 774 the kingdom had collapsed and the Franks ruled northern Italy. The Duchy of Benevento became the independent Principality of Benevento.

Charlemagne ruled northern Italy as King of the Lombards. In 781 he named his son Pepin King of Italy while keeping suzerainty over the land. From Louis the Pious in 818, the kingdom was ruled directly by the Carolingian Emperor himself.

When Emperor Lothair I died in 855, his realm of Middle Francia was split among his three sons under the Treaty of Prüm. The eldest, Louis II, received the imperial crown and Carolingian Italy, reaching as far south as Rome and Spoleto. The rest of southern Italy stayed under Benevento or the Byzantine Empire.

After Charles the Fat died in 887, Italy fell into instability as several kings tried to make themselves independent monarchs. This period is known as the Feudal Anarchy (888 to 962). During it the new title Rex Italicorum, meaning King of the Italians, was introduced.

Some of Italy's earliest medieval city-states began to emerge in the 7th century. The Duchy of Naples, the Duchy of Amalfi, Gaeta and the Republic of Venice were nominally under Byzantine control but effectively independent. The Duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, by contrast, were under Lombard control.

philosophy.text: Historians disagree about what happened to Rome's ancient religious traditions in the Christian centuries. One view stresses direct survival of ancient rites, another stresses reinterpretation and adaptation, and a third sees an ideological rupture. Together, these models describe how Roman paganism was gradually relocated and reworked within medieval Christian culture.

Boethius, who lived from 472 to 524 AD, is counted among the Roman philosophers of Italy. His life reached into the sixth century, making him a link between the ancient philosophical tradition and the early medieval world. Italian medieval philosophy would later be mainly Christian.

Boethius wrote On the Consolation of Philosophy in 523 during a one-year imprisonment, awaiting trial and eventual execution for alleged treason under the Ostrogothic King Theodoric the Great. The work reflects on how evil can exist in a world governed by God, and how happiness is still attainable amidst fickle fortune.

Boethius sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He aimed to translate the entirety of the Greek classics for Western scholars, and it is largely due to his translations that the works of Aristotle survived into the Renaissance.

In 589 King Reccared of the Visigoths moved Spain from Arianism to Catholic Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo. The council also enacted restrictions on Jews. Canon 14 forbade Jews to have Christian wives, concubines or slaves, ordered the children of such unions to be baptized, and barred Jews from any office in which they might have to punish Christians. The proscriptions were soon followed by required conversions, which caused a wholesale flight of Jews from Visigothic Spain to Ceuta and nearby territories in North Africa. The council is also known for codifying the filioque clause into Western Christianity, which caused controversy among the Franks and contributed to the Great Schism of 1054.

Charlemagne was advised by Candidus, Peter of Pisa and Alcuin of York, and by imperial decree in 787 he established schools in every abbey in his empire. These schools became centres of medieval learning, and the name Scholasticism is derived from them.

In the Consolation, Boethius answered religious questions without reference to Christianity, relying solely on natural philosophy and the Classical Greek tradition. He believed that the truths found in Christianity would be no different from the truths found in philosophy.

Cassiodorus saw the writings of the Greeks and Romans as valuable for expressing higher truths, though vastly inferior to the perfect word of Scripture. He was unafraid to cite Cicero alongside sacred text. Only Boethius rivalled his drive to preserve classical literature in the 6th century.

Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae summarized knowledge from hundreds of classical sources, covering among other things the church and heretical sects and pagan philosophers. It was so popular as a textbook that it was read in place of many of the original classics, and some of these ceased to be copied and were lost.

In the Consolation, Philosophy illustrates the capricious nature of Fate through the image of the wheel of Fortune, and argues that true happiness lies in the pursuit of wisdom. She also demonstrates that many earthly goods, such as wealth and beauty, are fleeting at best.

Boethius believed that arithmetic and music were intertwined, each reinforcing the understanding of the other. Together they exemplified the fundamental principles of order and harmony in the universe. His De institutione musica later helped ninth-century theorists understand ancient Greek music.

Cassiodorus spent his career trying to bridge the cultural divides of the 6th century: East and West, Greek and Latin, Roman and Goth, and an orthodox people and their Arian rulers. In his later years he devoted himself to Christian learning and founded the Vivarium monastery.

Before the Third Council of Toledo, King Reccared held assemblies where Arian and Catholic bishops presented their arguments. He pointed out that no Arian bishop had ever performed a healing miracle. At the last assembly, with only Catholic bishops present, he accepted the Catholic faith.

culture.text: The Arianist Visigoths ruled an Iberian kingdom from 507 to 711. They were converted to Catholicism along with their king Reccared in 587. Their culture can be seen as a phenomenon of Late Antiquity as much as part of the Age of Migrations.

After the fall of the western empire, the Church often became the only stable institution and the only source of learning in Western Europe. Even the barbarians had to rely on clerics to administer their conquests. Monastic orders such as the Benedictines helped preserve classical culture.

Between the 7th and 10th centuries, under Byzantine and Lombard rule, canon law records in Italy set out religious norms. These records reflect the coexistence of local beliefs and Christian rituals. They indicate that ritual practices of pagan origin survived alongside the Christian faith.

Four churches in Rome have mosaics of saints near where their relics were held, including San Lorenzo fuori le Mura (580s) and Santo Stefano Rotondo (640s). They abandon classical illusionism for large-eyed figures floating in space. Rome had been in Byzantine hands from 536-545, which may explain the change.
culture.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

culture.text: Political stability after the Frankish conquest of Italy brought a new burst of major Roman mosaics in the Carolingian period. Five Roman churches have mosaics from this time, including Santa Prassede and Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, both from about 820. Their semi-domes show Saints Peter and Paul presenting martyrs and a donor Pope carrying a model of the church.
culture.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

culture.text: In the 5th to 7th centuries, excavations at Crypta Balbi in Rome uncovered domestic layers containing reused cult objects, protective amulets and small figurative items. Archaeologists interpret them as remnants of late Roman ritual behavior. They show older religious practices lingering in the daily life of the city.

The Carolingian mosaics of Rome varied in design. Santi Nereo e Achilleo (c. 814) has an iconographically eccentric programme at its east end. Santa Maria in Domnica (c. 820) shows an enthroned Madonna and Child in the midst of saints and angels.
culture.source_title: Late Antique and medieval mosaics in Italy

culture.text: In the 7th–10th centuries, under Byzantine and Lombard rule, canon law records religious norms reflecting the coexistence of local beliefs and Christian rituals. This indicates that ritual practices of pagan origin survived in Italy.
